briefOverview: Jesus prays for his own glorification, for the protection and sanctification of his disciples, and for the unity and future of all who will believe through their message.
summary: Jesus addresses the Father, declaring that the hour has come and asking to be glorified so that he may glorify the Father, defining eternal life as knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He sent. He affirms that he has revealed the Father’s name to those given to him, who received and believed his words, and he prays specifically for them, not for the world. He asks the Father to keep them in His name, to unify them, to guard them from evil, and to sanctify them in the truth of God’s word; he notes that none were lost except the “son of perdition,” fulfilling Scripture. As the Father sent him, he sends them, consecrating himself so that they may be sanctified in truth. Extending beyond the immediate disciples, he prays for all future believers to be one, to share in the glory given, to be perfected in unity so the world may know the Father’s love and sending, and to be with him to behold his preexistent glory.
externalContext: This prayer concludes the Johannine Farewell Discourse (John 13–17), traditionally located on the night before Jesus’ arrest and crucifixion during the Passover festival. In Second Temple Jewish practice, lifting the eyes toward heaven was a known prayer posture, and invoking God’s “name” signified revealing God’s character and reputation. “Sanctify” (set apart for God) draws on temple and priestly language familiar to Jesus’ Jewish audience. The designation “High Priestly Prayer” is a later Christian title highlighting Jesus’ intercessory role for his followers.
externalReferences: The mention of the “son of perdition” and Scripture fulfillment echoes the earlier citation of Psalm 41:9 in John 13:18 concerning Judas’s betrayal. Jesus’ request to share the glory he had before the world existed resonates with John 1:1–2 and the incarnation theme of John 1:14. His commissioning of the disciples (“As you sent me, I have sent them”) is reiterated after the resurrection in John 20:21. The petition to be kept from evil parallels the Lord’s Prayer (“deliver us from evil”) in Matthew 6:13, and the emphasis on truth aligns with Jesus’ teaching in John 8:31–32.
practicalQuestions: How does my understanding of God and Jesus shape my view of eternal life now, not just in the future?
What would it look like in practice to be “in the world” but not “of the world” in my context?
How can I actively pursue unity with other believers without compromising truth?
In what concrete ways can I submit to God’s word so that it shapes my sanctification?
Where and to whom am I being sent, and how can my life and words help others believe that the Father sent the Son?
uncertainAreas: “World” could mean humanity in rebellion, the created order, or societal systems; the passage uses it in more than one sense. “Keep them from the evil” may mean from evil in general or from the evil one; the Greek allows both. The identity of the “son of perdition” is commonly understood as Judas, but the chapter does not name him explicitly. The nature of the “glory” shared with believers (22) is not specified—whether it is the Spirit’s presence, participation in divine mission, or eschatological glory remains interpretively debated.
